experiments.title: Which JSON library is fastest?
experiments.question: We have to send JSON (the usual web text). Each timed call is one shop order — an id, a status, and eight line items, about 450 bytes — not a file of many orders. Which JSON library is fastest?

story.why: Most websites already speak JSON. Changing that format is expensive. First we ask whether a faster JSON library is enough.
story.example: A shop’s public API sends one order as JSON. Partners and browsers already expect that text.
story.tradeoff: A faster library can help a lot. A library that checks types is slower on purpose — that extra time buys safety, not speed.

experiments.title: Should two services inside the company stop using JSON?
experiments.question: On one small record, how do JSON, MessagePack, and Protocol Buffers compare?

story.why: Inside a company you may pick a denser format. That is a real cost (new tools, harder debugging). We measure whether the gain is large.
story.example: Two services you own swap a small request on a private network. No browser is on this path.
story.tradeoff: JSON is easy to read at 3 a.m. The other two write smaller bytes. Protocol Buffers needs a shared field list. MessagePack does not.

experiments.title: Is a one-language format worth the lock-in?
experiments.question: On one small record, is a format only one language can read faster than a format other languages can read?

story.why: Formats like Python pickle are built for one language talking to itself. Next year another service may need the same bytes.
story.example: A cache or a job queue that “only we write today.” Next quarter a second program cannot open the key.
story.tradeoff: A one-language format can store rich objects. Other languages cannot read it. Some of these readers can run code — that is a safety problem.

experiments.title: When is JSON too big for a sensor?
experiments.question: As a list of sensor numbers grows, when does JSON no longer fit a small radio packet?

story.why: A radio packet has a size limit. JSON is easy to read but writes extra text around every number.
story.example: A device sends 8, then 32, then 128, then 512 readings. We mark two example limits: 128 bytes and 512 bytes.
story.tradeoff: Stay on JSON if it still fits, so people can read the packets. Leave JSON when the packet overflows and a denser format still fits.

experiments.title: What should we use for an event log?
experiments.question: On one “something happened” record, how do Avro, Protocol Buffers, and JSON compare on size and write time?

story.why: Event logs keep facts for months. Size drives disk cost. Write time drives the producer’s CPU. Compatibility (old and new software together) is why Avro and Protocol Buffers exist.
story.example: “Order placed” is written many times a day and stored for months. Outside parties still get JSON at the edge.
story.tradeoff: JSON is easy to read and can drift. Avro and Protocol Buffers are smaller. Speed cannot override a failed compatibility story.

experiments.title: Are database formats better for a normal service call?
experiments.question: On one order, do BSON, Smile, and Ion beat JSON and MessagePack when we write the whole record and read it all back?

story.why: BSON, Smile, and Ion were built for databases and skip-through documents, not for a simple “write it all, read it all” call.
story.example: A program talking to MongoDB (BSON) or Java services talking to Elasticsearch (Smile).
story.tradeoff: These formats spend bytes so a reader can skip a field. This test always reads the whole record, so that extra may look like a loss.

experiments.title: Fast to write, or fast to read?
experiments.question: If we build a record once and read it many times, how do FlatBuffers and Cap’n Proto split write time and read time?

story.why: Some libraries make reading cheap (look at the bytes as they arrived). Writing can be more expensive. Adding write + read hides that split.
story.example: A game asset, a replay file, or a buffer one program builds and another reads many times — sometimes only a few fields.
story.tradeoff: Good when you write once and read often. Poor when you change the record on every request. Look at write and read separately. Do not add them.

experiments.title: Can we send YAML on the live path?
experiments.question: On the same records, how much slower and larger are YAML, TOML, and XML than JSON?

story.why: YAML, TOML, and XML exist so people can edit files. They were not built for a live request.
story.example: A service reads a config file at start. Someone proposes sending that same YAML on every request.
story.tradeoff: Keep YAML on disk if people edit it. Convert once at start. Use JSON (or a denser format) on the live path.

experiments.title: Does squeezing the bytes make JSON small enough?
experiments.question: After gzip or zstd, does JSON stay larger than a dense binary format?

story.why: Teams often turn compression on for everything. It finds repeated words. Tiny messages can get slower, because the processor work exceeds the bytes you save.
story.example: A public web page (large text) versus a chatty internal ping (a few dozen bytes).
story.tradeoff: On repeated words, compression can pull JSON next to a dense format. On numbers, the format still matters. Do not compress tiny control calls.

experiments.title: Does one record rank the same as one hundred?
experiments.question: Does the library that is fastest for one record stay fastest when we write one hundred records at once?

story.why: A web call is usually one body. A log shipper often writes many records at once. Some libraries have a large cost every time you call them. That cost vanishes in a batch.
story.example: One “get user” request versus a telemetry exporter that sends 100 readings in one write.
story.tradeoff: Quote the number of records that matches the product. A chart of 100 records is not evidence for a one-record call.

experiments.title: Does writing to a file change the ranking?
experiments.question: When we write as if to a file, which libraries really write as they go, and does the ranking change?

story.why: A cache uses a block of bytes in memory. A file or socket writes as you go. Some “stream” numbers are a full result that is then copied.
story.example: Saving a cache key versus writing a file or a network socket.
story.tradeoff: Only treat a real stream path as evidence for a file. If the product is a cache, the in-memory number is the one that matters.

experiments.title: Is it the format, or the library?
experiments.question: If one library can write several formats, how much of the difference is the format, and how much is that library?

story.why: People say “we switched to binary” as if the name were the whole decision. Two libraries that both write JSON can still differ a lot.
story.example: Jackson in Java can write JSON, MessagePack, Smile, and more. We hold Jackson still and only change what it writes.
story.tradeoff: This tells you about that one library, not about every MessagePack library in the world. “Move to binary” without naming the library is not a plan.

experiments.title: Does the ranking stay the same if we change the data?
experiments.question: Do the ranks stay the same if we change the record, how many we write at once, or how we set aside odd trials?

story.why: One run on one computer is one evening’s measurement. A ranking that flips when we change the data or the cleaning rule was never a fact about the libraries.
story.example: The fastest JSON library on one order may not stay fastest on a list of words, or when we write 100 records at once.
story.tradeoff: A large gap that holds on every sample is a stable fact. A close contest that swaps places is too close to name a winner.
